examples.question_text: A cube is resting on one of its faces. Give a prism name for the cube and explain why it fits.
examples.solution_text: Two opposite faces are identical parallel squares. These can be its bases, so a cube is a **square prism**.

examples.question_text: A prism has $6$ rectangular side faces. What is its name?
examples.solution_text: Each side of a base meets one rectangular side face. The base therefore has $6$ sides: a hexagon. The solid is a **hexagonal prism**.

examples.question_text: A pyramid has $6$ faces altogether. Determine its name.
examples.solution_text:
One face is the base.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Triangular side faces} &= 6-1 \\ &= 5\end{aligned}$

Each triangular side face meets one side of the base. The base has $5$ sides, so the solid is a **pentagonal pyramid**.

examples.question_text: A prism has $8$ vertices. Determine its name.
examples.solution_text:
The vertices are shared equally between two identical bases.

$\begin{aligned}\text{Vertices on each base} &= 8\div2 \\ &= 4\end{aligned}$

Each base has $4$ sides, so the solid is a **quadrilateral prism**. The vertex count alone does not tell us whether the base is a square or a rectangle.

examples.question_text: A pentagonal prism is resting on a rectangular side face. Does its name change? Explain.
examples.solution_text: Its name stays **pentagonal prism**. Its two identical parallel bases are still pentagons; the face it rests on does not change its name.

The stated rectangular base and four triangular side faces meeting at one apex identify a rectangular pyramid. The diagram and solution agree with these properties.
A cube has opposite identical parallel square faces that can serve as its two bases, making square prism a valid name.
Six rectangular side faces correspond to six sides on each base. A six-sided base is a hexagon, so the solid is a hexagonal prism.
Subtract the single base from six total faces: 6−1=5 triangular side faces. These correspond to five base sides, giving a pentagonal pyramid. The aligned calculation needs no opening phantom equals.

Eight vertices divided equally between two bases give 8÷2=4 vertices per base. Each base is a quadrilateral, so quadrilateral prism is justified; square or rectangular cannot be inferred. The aligned calculation needs no opening phantom equals.
Changing the resting face leaves the two identical parallel pentagonal bases unchanged, so the name remains pentagonal prism.
